facts.claim: Georgia State University's Safe Night Out case follows startup co-founders Kris and Sandy to teach accounting decisions.
facts.mechanism: Because transactions change the fortunes of named people and their venture, accounting categories gain causal and narrative hooks.
facts.commonError: The Safe Night Out method removes financial statements and teaches only entrepreneurship anecdotes.
facts.whyWrong: The story supplies context for the accounting content; it does not replace the underlying concepts and records.

facts.claim: Jane Elliott first ran the blue-eyes/brown-eyes exercise with her Iowa third-grade class on April 5, 1968.
facts.mechanism: Because arbitrary eye color immediately changed status, privileges, and treatment, pupils encountered discrimination as an operating system rather than a vocabulary word.
facts.commonError: Elliott merely asked pupils to imagine discrimination without changing classroom roles.
facts.whyWrong: The exercise assigned superiority and disadvantage, then reversed the categories so pupils experienced both positions.

facts.claim: The Boeing 727 design criterion named a fully loaded takeoff and a safe landing on LaGuardia Runway 4-22.
facts.mechanism: Because the criterion specifies aircraft, load state, place, and runway, engineering teams can evaluate competing designs against the same outcome.
facts.commonError: The 727 teams coordinated around the unmeasurable instruction to build the world's best airplane.
facts.whyWrong: An abstract superlative permits conflicting interpretations, whereas the runway task supplies a common performance test.

facts.claim: Oral rehydration salts combine sugar and salts for dissolution in clean water to treat dehydration from fluid loss.
facts.mechanism: Because intestinal glucose transport remains coupled with sodium uptake during severe diarrhoea, the solution accelerates absorption of salt and water.
facts.commonError: Plain water alone replaces the electrolytes and uses the same intestinal transport mechanism as ORS.
facts.whyWrong: The therapeutic mechanism depends on correctly proportioned glucose and electrolytes, not water without solutes.

facts.claim: James P. Grant used a packet of sugar and salt as a concrete representation of oral rehydration therapy.
facts.mechanism: Because policymakers could see and hold the intervention's ingredients, a large public-health program became a graspable action rather than a remote abstraction.
facts.commonError: Grant's packet was offered as a complete dry medicine to swallow without water or measurement.
facts.whyWrong: The ingredients must be prepared as a correctly diluted oral solution; the packet represented the intervention, not a dry dose.

facts.claim: The Fox and the Grapes makes self-protective devaluation visible through a fox dismissing fruit it cannot reach.
facts.mechanism: Because the motive appears inside a physical failed attempt and a face-saving response, the abstract bias is easy to reconstruct later.
facts.commonError: The fable's mechanism is that unreachable objects objectively become lower quality.
facts.whyWrong: The fruit does not change; the fox changes its judgment to protect itself after failure.

facts.claim: Concrete language is expressed through sensory or observable terms that different listeners can picture or inspect.
facts.mechanism: Because observable referents constrain possible interpretations, people are more likely to attach the same meaning to the message.
facts.commonError: Concrete language is any sentence containing a large number, even when nobody can visualize its scale.
facts.whyWrong: A numeral can remain abstract; concreteness requires a perceptible referent, comparison, action, or test.

facts.claim: The Velcro theory of memory treats concrete details as multiple hooks that can cue later retrieval.
facts.mechanism: Because a scene can be reached through people, objects, sensations, actions, and consequences, forgetting one route need not erase the idea.
facts.commonError: Memory improves only when a message repeats the same abstract phrase many times.
facts.whyWrong: Repetition strengthens one route, while varied concrete hooks create several routes back to the same meaning.

facts.claim: Concrete criteria improve coordination by giving specialists a shared definition of completion.
facts.mechanism: Because each contributor can test work against the same observable result, disciplinary assumptions are less likely to produce incompatible outputs.
facts.commonError: Abstract goals coordinate experts better because each team can privately define success.
facts.whyWrong: Private definitions create hidden divergence; a common test exposes mismatches before integration.
